name: Oven and Pans
summary: Getting even heat from your oven, how the pan's size and material change a bake, and how to prep and cool it.

sections.heading: Preheat properly
blocks: Most bakes need a fully hot oven from the first minute: cookies set before they spread too far, and quick breads and cakes rise before their crust forms. An oven's ready signal usually means the air has reached the temperature; the walls and racks catch up later, so give it another 10–15 minutes.

blocks.text: Ovens are often off by 25°F (15°C) or more. A cheap oven thermometer on the middle rack tells you how yours runs; then set the dial higher or lower to match what the recipe asks for.

sections.heading: Rack position

items: **Middle rack** for nearly everything: the heat is most even there.
**Lower third** for pies and pizza, so the bottom crust gets more heat.
**Upper third** for browning a top at the end.

blocks: For the most even cookies, bake one sheet at a time in the middle. Baking two? Use the upper and lower thirds and swap and turn the sheets halfway through.

sections.heading: Convection
blocks: A convection (fan) setting blows the hot air around, which browns and bakes faster. When a recipe is written for a regular oven, lower the temperature by 25°F (15°C), or keep it and start checking a few minutes early. Some ovens make that adjustment for you; the manual says.

Baking at a different temperature for another reason, like sharing the oven with something else? The [Oven Time Converter](tool:/utils/oven-time) estimates the new time. It doesn't know about pan size, convection or how full the oven is: treat its time as the moment to start checking.

sections.heading: Pan material
blocks: Recipes assume a **light-colored metal** pan unless they say otherwise. Other pans bake differently:

rows: Absorbs more heat: darker bottoms and edges.
Lower the oven by 25°F (15°C), or check early.
Slow to heat, then holds heat: edges can overbake before the middle is done.
Set it on a baking sheet so it doesn't sag.

blocks.text: Don't move a hot glass dish onto a wet or cold surface, or put it under a broiler: a sudden temperature change can make it shatter.

sections.heading: Pan size
blocks: The recipe pages offer a pan picker on recipes baked in a pan, like [Banana Bread](recipe:banana-bread) and [Fudgy Brownies](recipe:brownies). It scales the batter to fill the pan you choose the same way the original fills its pan. What it can't do is change the bake time, because time depends on how deep the batter is:

items: **Deeper batter** (a smaller pan, or a loaf pan instead of a square one): longer bake, and the edges may finish before the middle. Lower the oven by 25°F (15°C) if the edges get too dark.
**Shallower batter** (a bigger pan): shorter bake. Start checking well before the recipe's time.
**Muffins from a loaf recipe:** much shorter. Banana Bread's tip gives 20–25 minutes instead of about an hour.

blocks: Whatever the pan, judge doneness by the signs in [Is It Done?](guide:baking-doneness), not the clock.

items: **Grease and flour** for cakes and quick breads: butter or spray the pan, add a spoonful of flour, tilt and tap until it's coated, and knock out the rest. Use cocoa instead of flour for chocolate bakes.
**Parchment sling** for brownies and bars: a strip of parchment that hangs over two sides, so you can lift the whole slab out to cut it.
**Parchment or a silicone mat** under cookies: they don't stick, and bottoms brown more evenly.
**Paper liners** for muffins, or grease the cups.

sections.heading: Cooling
blocks: Baking doesn't stop when the pan comes out: the heat stored in the pan keeps cooking. Set pans on a wire rack so air reaches the bottom, which also stops steam from making it soggy. How long to leave things in the pan is in [Is It Done?](guide:baking-doneness#cooling).
